conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really weak and dizzy for a few days. I had chills, sweats, and stomach pain. My blood sugar’s been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned nausea and watery diarrhea. Any fever at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had a fever up to 101. I’ve been using Compazine for the nausea, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We ran some blood tests when you arrived. Your glucose was very high—over 700—and we found ketones in your urine. You’re in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve been trying to keep up with my insulin. Why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know the exact trigger yet. It could be illness, stress, or insulin not getting absorbed well. But we’ve started IV fluids and a small dose of insulin, and your numbers are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired and anxious. I couldn’t sleep last night. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Benadryl and Dilaudid earlier. Ativan didn’t help, you said. We can restart your usual diazepam if you’d like—it’s on your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. The Benadryl helps me relax a bit, but I need the diazepam. And can I get Dilaudid again? The pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you Dilaudid as scheduled. We’re monitoring your pain and will keep using your regular home plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your anion gap has normalized, and your glucose is down to 180. That means the DKA is resolving. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my stomach still hurts, especially on the right side. Is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lipase—it’s normal. The ultrasound didn’t show gallstones or liver issues. Given your history, we think it’s likely related to your chronic pancreatitis, not an acute flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no change in my pain meds? I’m worried I won’t get enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home regimen—Dilaudid, gabapentin, and ibuprofen as needed. We’ll advance your diet today since your DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HbA1c came back at 9.3%. That confirms your sugars have been high over the last few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I struggle with it. But I take my glargine every night. Is that still the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re keeping you on your usual insulin—70 units at bedtime and the sliding scale. No changes, to avoid confusion when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit shaky. Is my potassium okay? I remember last time it dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. Your potassium was low this morning—3.0. We’re giving it through your IV to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take it by mouth instead? I don’t like NG tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You refused the NG tube, which is fine. We’re doing IV repletion only. We won’t force any tests or treatments you’re not comfortable with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were slightly high on admission, but that was likely from a hemolyzed blood sample. A repeat test was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my liver? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of liver disease. The ultrasound was clear, and your bile ducts are normal. Nothing concerning there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your glucose is stable, and you’ve been eating without nausea. We’re switching you back to oral meds completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite yet. We want to make sure your potassium stays up and you remain stable on your own insulin. Probably one more night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got upset yesterday when I couldn’t get my Dilaudid on time. I didn’t mean to yell. I just get anxious when my pain’s not controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We reviewed it—the team knows your needs. We also clarified your meds. Turns out you weren’t actually taking Actos, so we removed it from your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t even realize it was still listed. That could’ve caused problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your potassium is still 3.0. We’ll keep giving IV potassium and monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another blood draw. Can we skip the next check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You refused the repeat potassium check, and that’s noted. We’ll continue treatment but respect your decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve been stable overnight. Your glucose is 123, and you’re alert and eating well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Are my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no changes. You’ll go home on your usual insulin, pain meds, and other prescriptions. We added Prochlorperazine for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should follow up with my primary doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Please see your PCP soon to review everything. You’re doing much better. We’ll get the discharge papers ready.
